```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(VsusP)
```

# Model and selection rule

For a Gaussian linear model, let $Y$ be the response vector, $X$ the design
matrix and $\beta$ the coefficient vector:
\[
Y=X\beta+\epsilon,\qquad \epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_n).
\]
Here $n$ is the number of observations and $\sigma^2$ is the residual variance.
Shrinkage priors draw coefficients toward zero without setting them exactly to
zero. VsusP uses the sequential two-means (S2M) method of Li and Pati (2017,
Section 2.2.1) to select a subset from these posterior draws.

For each draw, S2M clusters absolute coefficients into two groups and saves the
lower-mean group as the noise candidate set $D$. While the center gap exceeds
$b$, it saves the current lower-mean group and splits that group again. When
the gap is at most $b$, it retains the saved $D$, giving signal count
$H=p-|D|$, where $p$ is the number of coefficients. VsusP also stops when the
candidate has at most two elements or identical magnitudes. It uses the modal
count across draws, then selects the $H$ largest posterior median absolute
coefficients. Equal-frequency modes favor the smaller count; equal medians
favor larger column indices.

# Installation

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("VsusP")
library(VsusP)
```

For the development version:

```{r github-install, eval=FALSE}
# Install devtools first if it is not available.
devtools::install_github("nilson01/VsusP-variable-selection-using-shrinkage-priors")
```

# Selection from posterior draws

The rows of `Beta` are posterior draws; columns correspond to coefficients.
Exclude any intercept column. These fixed draws show the selection steps
without fitting a regression model.

```{r draws}
Beta <- rbind(c(.01, .02, .03, .3, .31, 10, 11),
              c(-.01, -.02, -.03, -.3, -.31, -10, -11))
colnames(Beta) <- paste0("x", seq_len(ncol(Beta)))
set.seed(1)
result <- Sequential2MeansBeta(Beta, lower=.1, upper=.5, l=2)
data.frame(b=result$b.i, H=result$H.b.i)
```

`OptimalHbi()` displays this path. It does not select a threshold or compute an
optimal value. In this illustration, we use $b=0.5$ and its corresponding count.

```{r tuning-path, fig.width=5, fig.height=3, fig.cap="S2M signal counts for the fixed coefficient draws."}
OptimalHbi(result$b.i, result$H.b.i)
```

```{r selection}
H <- result$H.b.i[2]
indices <- S2MVarSelection(Beta, H)
colnames(Beta)[indices]
S2MVarSelectionV1(result, H)
```

Both selection functions return column indices. `S2MVarSelectionV1()` uses the
stored medians rather than recomputing them. `H=0` returns `integer(0)`; this is
an explicit selection count, not an empty-model decision made by S2M.

# Gaussian fitting with bayesreg

`Sequential2Means()` fits a Gaussian regression through `bayesreg` and applies
S2M to all returned coefficient draws. Its priors are `ridge` (`rr`), `lasso`,
`horseshoe` (`hs`) and `horseshoe+` (`hs+`). The intercept is excluded.

```{r fit, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(12)
X <- matrix(rnorm(120),40,3)
colnames(X) <- c("x1","x2","x3")
y <- 3*X[,1] + rnorm(40)
fit <- Sequential2Means(X,y,b.i=c(.1,.5),prior="ridge",
                        n.samples=100,burnin=100)
dim(fit$Beta)
S2MVarSelectionV1(fit,fit$H.b.i[1])
```

Use adequate sampling and check convergence before interpreting the results.
For draws from a separate `bayesreg` fit, transpose its coefficient matrix:

```{r separate-fit, eval=FALSE}
posterior <- bayesreg::bayesreg(y ~ .,data.frame(X,y),model="gaussian",
                               prior="horseshoe",n.samples=5000,burnin=2000,n.cores=1)
Beta <- t(posterior$beta)
result <- Sequential2MeansBeta(Beta,lower=.1,upper=.5,l=5)
```

# Gaussian fitting and prediction

The native samplers return coefficient draws, intercept draws and residual
variances with separate iteration and chain axes. `FitRidge()` draws independent
posterior samples. `FitHorseshoe()` and `FitSpikeSlab()` use iterative sampling.
They center $X$ and $Y$ without standardizing predictor columns. Their priors
are specified in `?FitGaussian` and differ from the `bayesreg` defaults.

```{r native-fit}
X.native <- cbind(x1=c(-2,-1,0,1,2,0), x2=c(0,1,-1,0,1,-1))
y.native <- c(-3,-1,0,1,3,.5)
native <- FitRidge(X.native,y.native,draws=1000,chains=2,seed=8)
summary(native)
dim(native$beta)
Beta.native <- PosteriorDraws(native)
dim(Beta.native)
```

`summary()` reports coefficient means, standard deviations and equal-tail
intervals. `PosteriorDraws()` pools the iteration and chain axes in its returned
matrix; the fitted object retains separate chains.

```{r coefficient-plot, fig.width=5, fig.height=3, fig.pos="H", fig.align="center", fig.cap="Posterior coefficient means and 95 percent equal-tail intervals in the ridge example. The dashed line marks zero."}
PlotCoefficients(native)
```

Predictors for new observations must have the same column definitions and
order. Prediction reuses posterior draws; it does not fit another model.

```{r native-prediction}
predict(native,X.native[1:2,,drop=FALSE])
predict(native,X.native[1:2,,drop=FALSE],include.noise=TRUE,seed=9)
```

The first call gives pointwise intervals for the conditional mean. The second
adds observation noise for posterior predictive intervals. Both report the same
posterior conditional mean.

```{r native-diagnostics}
if (requireNamespace("posterior",quietly=TRUE)) ChainDiagnostics(native)
```

`ChainDiagnostics()` uses the `posterior` package for rank R-hat, bulk and tail
effective sample sizes, and the Monte Carlo standard error of the mean. It
requires explicit chain identities and does not reconstruct chains from pooled
draws. A single chain has no R-hat; constant variables have unavailable
diagnostics. `PlotTrace()` and `PlotAutocorrelation()` display chains separately.
Finite diagnostics alone do not establish convergence.

The trace and autocorrelation plots below use the saved horseshoe example with
five observations and four chains. Each chain retains 3000 draws after 1000
burn-in iterations. The trace shows the first 300 retained draws; the
within-chain autocorrelations use all 3000.

```{r trace-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width="\\linewidth", fig.align="center", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="First 300 retained coefficient draws in four horseshoe chains. The short excerpt illustrates the display; it does not establish convergence."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(system.file("help","figures",package="VsusP"),"trace.pdf"))
```

```{r acf-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width="\\linewidth", fig.align="center", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Within-chain sample autocorrelations for the same coefficient, using 3000 retained draws per chain."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(system.file("help","figures",package="VsusP"),"autocorrelation.pdf"))
```

To summarize which coefficients are included, fit a spike-and-slab model:

```{r native-spike}
native.ss <- FitSpikeSlab(X.native,y.native,draws=200,burnin=100,chains=2,seed=4)
summary(SpikeSlabSelection(PosteriorDraws(native.ss)))
```

```{r inclusion-plot, fig.width=5, fig.height=3, fig.pos="H", fig.align="center", fig.cap="Inclusion frequencies from the short spike-and-slab example, with the median probability model cutoff at 0.5. The short run does not establish convergence."}
PlotInclusion(native.ss)
```

# SAVS and empty selections

With default handling, S2M leaves at least one signal. For a separate rule that can return no
variables, VsusP provides the signal adaptive variable selector (SAVS) of Ray
and Bhattacharya (2018). Let $\widehat\beta_j$ be a supplied coefficient estimate
and $X_j$ its predictor column. With $a_+=\max(a,0)$, their closed form is
\[
\widehat\beta_j^*=\operatorname{sign}(\widehat\beta_j)\|X_j\|^{-2}
\left(|\widehat\beta_j|\|X_j\|^2-|\widehat\beta_j|^{-2}\right)_+.
\]
An exactly zero estimate gives zero by continuity. A coefficient survives only
when $|\widehat\beta_j|^3\|X_j\|^2>1$; equality gives zero. Every coefficient
can therefore be removed. The implementation protects against overflow and uses
an explicit roundoff convention for numerically ambiguous extreme-scale scores.

```{r savs}
SAVS(diag(2),c(.1,-.1))$selected
SAVS(diag(2),c(2,0))$coefficients
SAVS(X.native,coef(native))$selected
```

Use the same predictor matrix and units that define the estimates, and exclude
the intercept. No scaling occurs inside `SAVS()`. Multiplying a predictor by a
factor and dividing its coefficient by that factor preserves the linear
predictor but changes the SAVS decision score. Standardize predictors before
fitting if selection on a common predictor scale is wanted. The closed form is
not the full penalized optimizer for correlated predictors and does not provide
an automatic false-discovery guarantee.

# DSS sparse prediction

To retain a short predictor list while approximating a fitted linear predictor,
`DSS()` uses the adaptive-L1 criterion of Hahn and Carvalho (2015,
equation 21). Let $\bar\beta$ be the posterior mean and let $X$ contain the
prediction points. We minimize over the sparse vector $\gamma$:
\[
\frac{1}{n}\|X\bar\beta-X\gamma\|_2^2
+\lambda\sum_{j:\bar\beta_j\ne0}\frac{|\gamma_j|}{|\bar\beta_j|},
\qquad \lambda\ge0.
\]
For $\lambda>0$, entries with $\bar\beta_j=0$ are constrained to zero.
For $\lambda=0$, the function returns $\bar\beta$.
This is the paper's convex approximation to its variable-count penalty.
The supplied $X$ may differ from the original fitting design, but its columns
must retain the same definitions and order. Keep the intercept separately.

```{r dss}
beta.mean <- coef(native)
dss <- DSS(X.native,beta.mean,lambda=.1)
dss$selected
dss$converged
penalties <- c(0,.01,.1,1,10)
dss.path <- lapply(penalties,function(lambda)DSS(X.native,beta.mean,lambda))
stopifnot(all(vapply(dss.path,function(x)x$converged,logical(1))))
data.frame(lambda=penalties,
           selected=vapply(dss.path,function(x)length(x$selected),integer(1)),
           mse=vapply(dss.path,function(x)x$mse,numeric(1)))
```

The penalty $\lambda$ controls the trade-off between sparsity and approximation
error; the function does not choose it automatically. The reported `mse`
compares $X\bar\beta$ with $X\gamma$ at the supplied points. It is not an
estimate of error on new outcomes. Coordinate descent reports its relative
optimality error as `kkt.error`; a warning and `converged=FALSE` identify an
unmet tolerance. Dependent columns can give different selected sets with the
same optimal fitted values. No inclusion probabilities or false-discovery
control are claimed.

# Clustering and tuning sensitivity

The default S2M path retains `kmeans` and the legacy small-set convention.
Two optional choices make computational decisions explicit:

* `clustering="exact"` minimizes the two-cluster within-group sum of squares
  over distinct adjacent cuts in sorted coefficient magnitudes. It uses no
  random initialization. Extreme numerical ranges that erase distinctions
  between inputs are rejected.
* `small.set="refine"` splits a distinct recursive pair and applies the same
  strict gap comparison. The default `"legacy"` retains that pair. This choice
  can change the final signal count.

```{r pair-refinement}
pair <- matrix(c(0,.125,10),nrow=1)
Sequential2MeansBeta(pair,.1,.1,1,"exact","legacy")$H.b.i
Sequential2MeansBeta(pair,.1,.1,1,"exact","refine")$H.b.i
```

For a threshold grid, `S2MSensitivity()` reports modal counts, their frequencies
and selected-set overlap. Jaccard similarity is the size of the intersection
of adjacent selected sets divided by the size of their union.

```{r sensitivity}
path <- S2MSensitivity(Beta,c(.1,.5),clustering="exact",small.set="refine")
data.frame(b=path$b.i,H=path$H.b.i,mode=path$mode.proportion,
           overlap=path$jaccard.previous)
```

Count frequencies are not inclusion probabilities. An exact clustering optimum
or stable selected set does not establish that the selected variables are correct.
Neither option chooses an optimal threshold.

# Spike-and-slab posterior draws

A spike-and-slab fit gives an exact zero for each excluded coefficient.
`SpikeSlabSelection()` uses these zeros to estimate inclusion probabilities:

```{r spike-slab}
Beta.ss <- rbind(c(1,0,0), c(2,0,0), c(0,-1,0), c(0,0,0))
colnames(Beta.ss) <- c("x1","x2","x3")
ss <- SpikeSlabSelection(Beta.ss)
ss$inclusion.probability
ss$MPM
ss$HPPM
```

These fixed draws illustrate the input. Replace them with posterior draws from
a spike-and-slab fit, excluding the intercept. The median probability model
(MPM) includes coefficients with inclusion frequency at least 0.5. The empirical
highest posterior probability model (HPPM) is the most frequent complete model
visited by the supplied draws. It need not be the most probable model over all
possible models. Tied model frequencies favor the first visited model; all tied
model indices are returned. Small continuous-prior coefficients are not spikes.

`TwoMeansBeta()` implements the basic 2-M rule: for each draw, take the smaller
of the two cluster sizes, then use the modal count and median absolute
coefficients to select variables. This differs from S2M's lower-mean noise set.

```{r spike-clustering}
TwoMeansBeta(Beta.ss)$selected
Sequential2MeansBeta(Beta.ss,.1,.5,2,clustering="exact",zero.draws="empty")
```

An entirely zero draw has no two-means split. `TwoMeansBeta()` assigns it zero
signals. S2M does so only with `zero.draws="empty"`; its default still rejects
such draws. These are explicit boundary extensions. Nonzero constant-magnitude
draws remain invalid. Median-ranking ties can select a coefficient never
included in any draw when all posterior medians are zero. Use the inclusion
summaries when inclusion probability is the quantity of interest.

# Selection performance in a small pilot

A reproducible pilot used 60 Gaussian datasets, with 10 datasets in each of six
conditions. Each had $n=80$, $p=10$ and residual standard deviation one.
The first two coefficients were $(0,0)$, $(0.25,-0.25)$ or $(1,-1)$; the others
were zero. Predictors had AR(1) correlation $\rho=0$ or $0.8$ and were centered
and standardized by their sample standard deviations before generating responses.
Horseshoe fits used one worker, 1,000 retained draws, burn-in 500 and thinning 5.

```{r pilot-table, echo=FALSE}
pilot <- read.csv(system.file("validation","summary.csv",package="VsusP"),check.names=FALSE)
pilot <- pilot[pilot$method=="SAVS",]
knitr::kable(pilot[,c("effect","rho","n_success","empty.mean","fp.mean","fn.mean","exact.mean")],
             col.names=c("Effect","Correlation","Datasets","Empty","FP","FN","Exact"),digits=2,row.names=FALSE)
```

Here Empty and Exact are proportions of datasets with an empty selection or
exactly the true variable set. FP and FN are mean counts of false positives and
false negatives. There were no failed fits or recorded warnings. SAVS returned
an empty set in all 20 null datasets, but it missed weak signals, especially
in the correlated opposite-sign case. The pilot is small: a proportion of
10/10 has a 95% Wilson interval of about 0.72 to 1.00.

```{r pilot-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width="\\linewidth", fig.cap="Empty selections and exact-support recovery across 10 datasets per condition, with 95 percent Wilson intervals. Labels give the first coefficient (the second is its negative) and predictor correlation. S2M thresholds are fixed, not optimized."}
source(system.file("validation","plot-selection-pilot.R",package="VsusP"))
pilot.figure <- tempfile(fileext=".pdf")
plot_selection_pilot(system.file("validation","summary.csv",package="VsusP"),pilot.figure)
knitr::include_graphics(pilot.figure)
```

Paired predictor-unit changes altered some SAVS selections while preserving the
fitted linear predictor. Undoing those changes restored the original selections
in every case. Selection based on the first and second posterior halves differed
in 2 of 60 cases. This comparison is an instability screen, not a convergence
check. The pilot does not establish false-discovery control or general accuracy.
The complete outcomes and runner are installed under `validation/`.

# Fixed-posterior checks

To check the native horseshoe and spike-and-slab fits, we compare their sampled
posterior summaries with independent numerical integration for the same
five-observation, one-predictor input. Each fit uses four chains, 1000 burn-in
iterations and 3000 retained draws per chain. We compare coefficient means and
mean residual variance; the spike-and-slab check also compares inclusion
probability. These fixed inputs test the fitted posterior calculations rather
than selection accuracy across repeated datasets.

```{r target-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width="\\linewidth", fig.align="center", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Sampled-minus-integrated summaries divided by the comparison tolerance: the larger of 0.01 and six Monte Carlo standard errors from 100-draw batches. HS denotes horseshoe and SS spike-and-slab. Shading marks the comparison criterion, not a confidence interval."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(system.file("help","figures",package="VsusP"),"posterior-agreement.pdf"))
```

```{r model-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width="\\linewidth", fig.align="center", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Spike-and-slab inclusion-state probabilities from numerical integration and sampling, with plus or minus 1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors. The trace excerpt shows the first 300 retained draws per chain; all 3000 enter the summaries."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(system.file("help","figures",package="VsusP"),"joint-models.pdf"))
```

The displayed differences meet the stated comparison tolerances. Agreement in this
small example does not establish reliable mixing in high-dimensional models or
interval coverage across repeated datasets. The numerical inputs and figure
source are supplied in `doc-data/`.

# Interpretation and limits

The threshold $b$ is on the coefficient scale. Scaling predictors changes its
meaning, so inspect the tuning path and sensitivity to scaling and $b$.
`kmeans` initialization can affect results; set a random seed for reproducibility.

S2M requires at least two coefficients and at least two distinct absolute values
in each initial draw. An initial pair of distinct values gives one noise
coefficient and one signal. Constant-magnitude draws are rejected because they
have no lower-mean cluster. After an initial split, an indivisible lower-mean
candidate is retained without another split.

By default, every accepted draw leaves at least one signal, so S2M cannot automatically
select an empty model. Its modal counts and selected variables are clustering
summaries. They are not posterior inclusion probabilities, significance tests or
a guarantee of false-positive control.
